mcqs.question: What caused Dennard scaling to break down around the mid-2000s?
options: Voltage could no longer scale down proportionally with transistor size, since lower voltage caused excessive leakage current and unreliable switching
Transistors stopped getting smaller with each process generation
Clock speeds were artificially capped by regulation
Manufacturers switched entirely to a different transistor material
mcqs.explanation: The breakdown was specifically a voltage-scaling limit: transistors kept shrinking, but voltage stopped shrinking with them, because lower voltage made leakage and reliability problems too severe. It wasn't a halt in transistor scaling itself, a regulatory cap, or a general material change.

mcqs.question: Why did the industry pivot to multicore designs once single-core clock speed hit its power wall?
options: Multicore designs are always more power-efficient than single-core designs at any clock speed
Adding more cores lets total throughput grow using more transistors, roughly within the same power envelope, when a single core can no longer get faster without exceeding the power budget
Multicore designs eliminate the need for cache coherence
Multicore was chosen purely for marketing reasons, not technical ones
mcqs.explanation: With single-core clock speed capped by power/thermal limits, using additional transistor budget for more cores (rather than a faster single core) became the way to keep raising throughput within a similar power envelope — provided software can actually use the parallelism. Multicore doesn't eliminate coherence (if anything it requires it), and the shift was a direct technical response to the Dennard breakdown, not a marketing choice.

mcqs.question: When does a "race to idle" DVFS strategy tend to beat running at a sustained lower power level throughout a task?
options: Race to idle always wins regardless of the device's idle power characteristics
Only when the task is purely compute-bound
When the device's idle power state draws much less power than its active state, so finishing fast and then sleeping saves more total energy
Only on desktop systems, never on mobile or battery-powered devices
mcqs.explanation: The strategy's payoff depends entirely on how cheap idle really is: if a deep sleep state draws far less power than active operation, sprinting to finish and then sleeping wins on total energy. If idle isn't much cheaper than active, sustained lower power can win instead — it isn't a universal rule, isn't tied to whether a task is compute-bound, and is actually especially relevant on mobile/battery devices, not excluded from them.

mcqs.question: A CPU's turbo-boost mode raises its clock speed for a few seconds under load, then drops back down even though the workload hasn't changed. What's the most likely explanation?
options: A software bug in the operating system's scheduler
Turbo boost is only cosmetic and never actually changes the real clock speed
The workload became less demanding, so a lower clock was appropriate
The chip hit its thermal or power-delivery budget and throttled the clock back down to stay within safe limits
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly thermal/power throttling: turbo boost is a burst capability bounded by the chip's power and thermal budget, not a sustained free upgrade, so sustained high load forces the clock back down once that budget is exhausted. It isn't a scheduler bug, the workload description says demand hasn't changed, and turbo boost genuinely changes the real clock speed while it's active.

mcqs.question: What does 'dark silicon' refer to, and why did it become a real design constraint?
options: Silicon defects that appear as literal dark spots on the die during manufacturing
Transistor count kept growing after Dennard scaling ended, but the power-per-area budget did not, so chips now have more functional units than they can power on simultaneously
A marketing term with no real hardware design implication
Cores that are permanently disabled due to a manufacturing yield issue
mcqs.explanation: Post-Dennard, transistor budgets kept growing (Moore's Law continued) but power density no longer shrank with them, so a chip can fit more units than it can afford to run at once without exceeding its thermal budget. This is a direct consequence of the same power wall that ended Dennard scaling, not a manufacturing defect or marketing term.

mcqs.question: A 150W chip has 30W fixed uncore draw and 15W per core at full clock. Why can't all 16 cores on such a chip run simultaneously at full rated clock speed?
options: Uncore power scales with core count, leaving no budget for any cores at all
The chip physically only has 8 functional cores despite being labeled 16-core
Only 120W remains for cores after the fixed 30W, enough for 8 cores at full clock -- running all 16 requires reducing per-core power (and clock) via DVFS to stay within budget
Power budgets only apply to single-core workloads, not multi-core ones
mcqs.explanation: 120W of core budget divided by 15W per core supports only 8 cores at full clock. Running all 16 simultaneously means each gets roughly half that power budget, forcing a lower clock via DVFS -- the power budget, not raw transistor or core count, is the real ceiling on simultaneous full-speed operation.
